title: Gentile sages were not crude corporealists—they used images as thin symbolic signs, yet still fell under Paul’s charge
source_text: XIX. Nec est quod quis regerat, sapientium illorum ex gentibus stultitiam in eo fuisse, non quod simpliciter Deo imagines collocarent, sed quod fingentes Deum corporeum, & membris variis distinctum, similem illum putarent, quoad externam formam, hominum, vel brutorum variorum imaginibus. Quicquid enim esse possit de rudi & Ethnica plebe, & de Epicureis Deo illi suo inerti, nec colendo, humanam similem formam tribuentibus, certum est illos gentium sapientes, de quibus agit Apostolus, qui Deum sub variis brutorum, vel hominum figuris exprimabant, ut in iis Deum colerent, ac praesertim Aegyptios, ad quos speciatim respicere videtur, non existimasse hominum, vel brutorum simulachra, quae Deo consecrabant, quoad externam formam, & corporis lineamenta, similia Deo fuisse, sed solum tenuiter, & symbolice Deum adumbrasse, ac fuisse duntaxat numinis tenues similitudines, & obscura signa, ut loquuntur Plutarchus, & Maximus Tyrius.
pass_a_gloss: Nor is there reason for anyone to retort that the folly of those wise men from the Gentiles was in this, not that they simply placed images for God, but that, fashioning God as corporeal, and distinct with various members, they thought him like, as to external form, to the images of men, or of various brutes. For whatever may be of the rude and Ethnic crowd, and of the Epicureans attributing a form like the human to that inert God of theirs, not to be cultivated, it is certain that those wise men of the Gentiles, of whom the Apostle treats, who expressed God under various figures of brutes or of men, that in them they might cultivate God, and especially the Egyptians, to whom he seems particularly to look, did not reckon that the simulacra of men or of brutes which they consecrated to God were, as to external form and the lineaments of the body, like to God, but only that they thinly and symbolically shadowed God, and were only thin likenesses of the divinity, and obscure signs, as Plutarch and Maximus of Tyre speak.
pass_b_english: Don’t rescue Romans 1 by saying only crude corporealists are meant.
Egypt’s sages treated images as thin symbolic signs—not literal God-bodies—and Paul still brands that folly.
